name: Dan Crenshaw

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: PET AND LIVESTOCK PROTECTION ACT
statements.title: PET AND LIVESTOCK PROTECTION ACT
sentences: Mr. Speaker, polls indicate that more than 70 percent of Americans support a full ban on puberty blockers for minors.
That is just about puberty blockers.
There is gender- affirming care.
These are kids suffering from teenage angst, and I don't deny the existence of gender dysphoria.
The highest quality medical reviews have consistently found no clear evidence that puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones, or surgeries reduce suicide risk in minors--none.
Puberty blockers are not approved by the FDA for treating gender dysphoria.
Cross-sex hormones can permanently compromise fertility.
Nearly every child placed on puberty blockers proceeds with the cross-sex hormones.
The United Kingdom now limits puberty blockers.
Children suffering from gender dysphoria deserve care, dignity, and clinical compassion, but that compassion does not mean pushing them on a medical pathway that leads to irreversible physical harm.
The Do No Harm in Medicaid Act draws a very clear moral line that the government will not participate in, endorse, or normalize irreversible gender surgeries and chemical interventions on minors.

Medicaid won't fund this abomination, but contrary to what many of the claims are, it preserves narrow exceptions for genuine medical conditions, like early onset puberty, disorders of sex development, and treatment of complications.
Mr. Speaker, I urge my colleagues to support the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act, please.
Chloe Cole spoke at the Department of Health and Human Services just now, about an hour ago.
Chloe Cole, at 12 years old, was going through what a lot of 12-year-olds are going through.
She is put on puberty blockers and soon on high levels of testosterone.

That is because I couldn't tell if that speech about harming kids was about our bill or about the act of conducting irreversible physiological changes on children who are going through gender dysphoria.
Mr. Speaker, this claim is made over and over, that allowing gender-affirming care, as they call it, is saving lives.
Mr. Speaker, 61 systematic studies concluded there is great uncertainty about the effects of puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones, and surgeries in young people.
A 2021 systematic review concluded that based on available data, no conclusions can be drawn about whether hormones, puberty blockers, or surgeries reduced suicide risk.
Again, in 2024, another independent review found that Britain's post- 2020 restriction of puberty blockers did not cause a rise in suicides despite many of the lies told on social media by activists.

A Johns Hopkins systematic review found that the evidence supporting claims that hormonal treatments may improve quality of life, depression, and anxiety among transgender patients was ``low.'' The study called for more research, particularly on adolescents.

Even a review published by the American Academy of Pediatrics, which institutionally has supported gender transition, admits that ``evidence regarding the psychosocial and cognitive impact of hormonal treatments for transgender adolescents is generally lacking.'' I could keep going.
They are talking about puberty blockers and hormonal therapies that permanently change the physiology of a young person before they are old enough to even understand what they might want in 20 years.
Again, on this idea that puberty blockers for children are safe and effective, let me read some more facts.

The Center for Investigative Reporting found that the FDA received over 10,000 adverse event reports from women who took Lupron, which is a common puberty blocker, off-label as children, to help them grow taller.
We are talking about Federal funding, Medicaid funding provided by the Federal Government.
We have heard that so-called gender-affirming care is necessary, effective, prevents suicides, and helps vulnerable children.

On hormonal treatments for transgender adolescents, APA said: ``Evidence regarding their psychosocial and cognitive impact is generally lacking.'' I get that their leadership is saying one thing, but the scientists are all saying something else.

As responsible policymakers, we might want to take a pause before we just go on and assume that permanent physiological changes to children are a good idea because they are going through something tough, whether that is gender dysphoria, teenage angst, depression, or anxiety.
Compassion is not a doctor lying to a child's parents about junk science in studies that say they won't have any remorse, that they will be fine, that puberty blockers are like a pause button.
It simply says that your tax dollars won't allow this to be done on minors, just your Medicaid tax dollars.
Mr. Speaker, I will not be long.
I will just ask a simple question, because the statement was made that all the science suggests that these procedures are medically necessary.
Mr. Speaker, I will cite mine.
I will again read the quote from the American Academy of Pediatrics when they did a review.

Here is the thing: The agency's own data found that our existing standards already kept those emissions in check and protect public health.
Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of H.J. Res. 61 because it is common sense.
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to stand with Chairman Griffith in support of this resolution.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: HALT ALL LETHAL TRAFFICKING OF FENTANYL ACT
statements.title: HALT ALL LETHAL TRAFFICKING OF FENTANYL ACT
sentences: Mr. Speaker, I rise today in strong support of the HALT Fentanyl Act because it is the most obvious thing in the world to be in support of.
It is the Mexican drug cartels.
We cannot let that expire because then we take away the tools that our prosecutors and law enforcement need to stop this deadly threat.
You need higher penalties for dealing fentanyl, a heck of a lot higher than the mandatory minimums we are even talking about here, if we actually care about saving kids' lives.
Everyone says, well, if we schedule this as a schedule I drug, then we are going to go right back to the old days of the 1980s and 1990s of mass incarceration.
I urge my colleagues to support this bill.
